subject: 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??

messages.author: a997b66afa263bd1
messages.subject: 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??
parts:
Hi Stan Gurus!

I am very new to STAN (like 2 weeks new) , and have been testing models with small 1000 row datasets which were taking ~5 minutes to run. Now I am fitting 10k data row (which is still about only 5% of my entire data set) , and it took me whole 15 hours to run ! There are 656 groups in the 'level 2' of the hierarchy so I know that has been contributing to the run time but I still feel its excessive. ( My system has 16GB RAM if that matters). Could someone look over my stan code (attached) and point out if their are any obvious time consuming bits which can be changed? Thanks for your help!!!

Edited to add:
iter=1000. Chains=3.The maximum n_eff that I can see is 1500.......many parameters have a single digit n_eff though.

Regards

messages.author: b17f4d0880547804
messages.subject: Re: 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??
parts:
How many iterations are you running it for?
What is the effective sample sizes you are getting? When does it look like it is converging?
In case you don't know stan's sampler is more efficient then what you get with the standard Gibbs sampler in BUGs and JAGS. Many stan models converge within a few hundred iterations...

However quickly scanning your code. You can vectorise the sampling statements.

For example:

  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(a[condolist[n]] +beta[condolist[n]][1] * x[n,1] +beta[condolist[n]][2] * x[n,2] +beta[condolist[n]][3] * x[n,3], sigma_y);
  
}

can become

for (n in 1:N) {
y_hat <- a[condolist[n]] +beta[condolist[n]][1] * x[n,1] +beta[condolist[n]][2] * x[n,2] +beta[condolist[n]][3] * x[n,3];
}
y ~ normal(y_hat, simga_y);

I haven't used the multi distributions... but they are likely to be vectorised too I think.

You should see a decent speed increase by doing this.

You could also look at lowering your stepsize to speed up adaption.

parts:
Hi Upasana,
It would also help sampling efficiency if you put weakly informative priors on your scale parameters (Simga_a, Sigma_y).
cauchy(0, 2.5) has worked well on several of my own models.
 
Also do you really expect gamma to vary from -200 to 200 as implied by the normal(0,100)?
If not maybe constrain it to what is biologically realistic.
J

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??
parts:
Great advice from James Camac.

A remaining drag in your code is this:

model {
matrix[M,M] Sigma_beta;
Sigma_beta <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(100.0, M));

...

for (j in 1:J)
beta[j] ~ multi_normal((u[j] * gamma)', Sigma_beta);

Two key pieces of advice:

1. Always vectorize for speed.

2. Never use a diagonal covariance matrix.

You should replace all of the above with:

for (j in 1:J)
beta[j] ~ normal(u[j] * gamma, 100);

You can make that even more efficient by following the advice in the
arrays and vectors chapter of the manual --- Here making u an array
of row vectors is ideal --- it avoids the copy and memory non-locality
problems of pulling out a row of a vector.

And two more as an added bonus:

3. Never use exp() if you can avoid it.

4. Never recompute subexpressions.

So your

mu[i] <- exp(b0 + log(i) * b
+ a[i]
+ theta * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
+ psi * a[i - 1] * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1]));

...
y ~ poisson(mu);

should define log_mu instead of mu and then use the Poisson taking
a log-scale parameter:

...
log_mu[i] <- exp(b0 + log(i) * b
+ a[i]
+ theta * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
+ psi * a[i - 1] * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1]));
..
y ~ poisson_log(log_mu);

Also, you want to assign the value of (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
to a local variable and reuse it in both places.

That should speed things up a lot, but won't help with statistical
efficiency. For that, you're going to need better priors or look
for places log_mu might be non-identified and causing problems,
as in adding b0 and a[i].

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??
parts:
> On Jul 13, 2015, at 2:03 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> I learned your words, Bob, by heart "you should be scared about exp" and it gave me good guidance so far. But, I wonder in this context:
>
> - what makes exp so terrible?

Underflows to 0 below about -700, overflows to +inf above 700 or
so and huge derivatives for values much greater than 0.

And it's expensive to compute.

But it's mainly that you don't want to have round trips of log
and exp, as you just lose arithmetic accuracy. If you do
everything on the log scale, which is where we need to wind up
eventually, it's much more robust.

For instance, check out

y ~ poisson_log(alpha)

vs.

y ~ poisson(exp(alpha))

The latter evaluates to

y * log(exp(alpha)) - lgamma(y + 1) - exp(alpha)

If we use a log-scale, we can avoid the round trip of log(exp(...)),
which accounts for about half of the computation (because the lgamma(y + 1) just
drops out because y is an integer and the (multiply and subtract are nearly free
relative to log and exp).

y ~ poisson_log(alpha)

just having to do

increment_log_prob(Y * alpha - exp(alpha));

So you still are going to have problems with overflow and underflow if
alpha is too far away from 0. But then that implies a Poisson with a mean
above 2 billion :-)
> - does it make a difference if I calculate in log space or on the natural space?
Algebraically, no. Arithmetically, yes. Log scale won't underflow or overflow.
> I mean I can define stuff to be log-normally distributed and then compute my means on the natural scale or I can use normals, but then do the computation in log-space.

Yes, but you have to consider the entire round trip out to unconstrained
parameters and back. If you have a parameter with lower=0, then it's
log transformed, with an explicit exp() on the way back from unconstrained
to constrained. There's no way to completely get rid of it if you need
a positive-constrained variable.
> Does the choice of what is better depend on what error model I use (proportional for log-space or additive for natural space).

Yes, as far as regression is concerned.

But all I was talking about was keeping the same model, but staying
on the log scale as much as possible.

- Bob
